name: tonic (Rust gRPC server) vs gRPC C++ in grpc_bench
baseline: gRPC C++ (grpc++ from the Debian libgrpc++-dev package) served by the grpc_bench cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_grpc_st servers, (cpp_grpc_mt Dockerfile: g++ -O3 -flto with jemalloc)
workload: Unary gRPC calls in the complex_proto scenario of LesnyRumcajs/grpc_bench: ghz client with 50 connections and 1000 concurrent requests, 120 s run after 30 s warmup, server limited to 1 to 4 CPUs.
claimed_speedup: Run of 2026-04-23 (server limited to 1 CPU): rust_tonic_st 102754 req/s vs cpp_grpc_st 57140 req/s (1.8x, derived from page data); rust_tonic_mt 82515 vs cpp_grpc_mt 57403 (1.44x, derived from page data). With 4 server CPUs: rust_tonic_mt 136638 req/s vs cpp_grpc_mt 85485 (1.6x, derived from page data), average latency 5.64 ms vs 11.28 ms. With 1 CPU the multithreaded tonic p99 latency is worse (98.22 ms vs 21.81 ms).
compiler_and_flags: C++ server (cpp_grpc_mt Dockerfile opened): gcc 16.1.0 image, g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto, linked to jemalloc and the distro libgrpc++-dev. Rust server (rust_tonic_mt Dockerfile and Cargo.toml opened): rust:1.94 image, cargo build --release with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, tikv-jemallocator, tonic 0.14, tokio 1.52. The _st variants' Dockerfiles were not opened.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (16 CPUs) @ 2.8 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.3, kernel 6.8.0-71, Digital Ocean dedicated server; client limited to 11 CPUs
stars_or_usage: 12.5k stars; about 422M crates.io downloads; grpc_bench harness has 939 stars
tradeoffs: Rust async stack (tokio, hyper, h2, prost). Only unary RPC is benchmarked; streaming, interceptors and the wider feature set of gRPC C++ are not compared. The multithreaded tonic server shows much worse tail latency than gRPC C++ when the server is limited to 1 CPU.
caveats: Application code is compiled with matching -O3 and LTO on both sides, but the gRPC C++ library is the distro binary package (not rebuilt at -O3 or with LTO), while tonic and its dependencies are built from source with LTO, so opt levels are not fully matched. The benchmark result is a user-submitted GitHub discussion post, not peer reviewed, one machine, one scenario. The C++ servers are community-contributed in the same repo and cpp_grpc_st uses a single thread (flat 57k req/s across CPU counts), so the server threading design rather than the language may drive the gap. The source states no mechanism; any explanation (async tokio/hyper HTTP/2 stack versus the C++ library's threading model) would be inference. The rust_grpcio row (Rust binding over the C core) is slower than cpp_grpc_mt at 1 CPU (50900 vs 57403 req/s) and faster from 3 CPUs (112812 vs 81581), which hints that threading model, not language, matters.
found_via: crates.io API keyword listings sorted by downloads (tonic, description 'focused on high performance'); then github.com LesnyRumcajs/grpc_bench discussion 559 (2026-04-23 results) and the Dockerfiles in that repo

name: Vector (Rust) vs Fluent Bit (C) in the Vector test harness
baseline: Fluent Bit 1.1.0 (C log forwarder); the same table also lists Filebeat, Fluentd, Logstash, Splunk UF and HF, which are not C/C++
workload: End-to-end log pipeline throughput in the vector-test-harness: TCP to blackhole, file to TCP, TCP to HTTP, TCP to TCP, and regex parsing, each run for 60 s on AWS instances with a separate producer instance.
claimed_speedup: README Comparisons table: TCP to Blackhole 86 MiB/s vs Fluent Bit 64.4 MiB/s (1.34x, derived from page data); File to TCP 76.7 vs 35 MiB/s (2.2x, derived); TCP to HTTP 26.7 vs 19.6 MiB/s (1.36x, derived); TCP to TCP 69.9 vs 67.1 MiB/s (parity, Splunk UF wins at 70.4); Regex Parsing 13.2 vs 20.5 MiB/s (Vector slower).
tradeoffs: Full observability pipeline (agent and aggregator) with a transform language; heavier on CPU than the simple C forwarder in the TCP to Blackhole case (max user CPU 96.5 vs 53.2) but lighter on memory there (181 MiB vs 614.8 MiB).
caveats: First-party harness; the TCP to Blackhole case README lists fluentbit 1.1.0 and vector 0.2.0-6-g434bed8 (the versions behind the other rows were not checked), so the numbers are very old; the harness README states it is under construction and some performance tests may be broken. Results do not state instance type, CPU model, compiler or flags (instance types are Terraform variables). Vector loses the regex parsing test and ties TCP to TCP. The comparison is between whole products with different feature sets, not an equal algorithm. The vector-test-harness case README for tcp_to_blackhole was opened (raw.githubusercontent.com) and its numbers match the vector README row; the other case READMEs were not compared line by line.
found_via: Brainstormed from popular Rust tools on crates.io and GitHub; opened the vectordotdev/vector README Comparisons table and the vector-test-harness case READMEs

name: Sambamba (D) vs samtools (C) for BAM processing
workload: SAM/BAM operations (flagstat, index, markdup, view, sort) run through the guigolab/sambamBench-nf Nextflow pipeline on a CRG cluster node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB memory, as summarised in the Sambamba README.
claimed_speedup: README (quoting a CRG sambamBench-nf comparison): 'for flagstat, Sambamba is 1.4x faster than samtools. For index, they are similar. For markdup, almost 6x faster, and for view, 4x faster. For sort, Sambamba has been beaten, though Sambamba is notably up to 2x faster than samtools on large RAM machines (120GB+).'
compiler_and_flags: Sambamba built with LDC (1.32.0 / LLVM 14 for release 1.0.0 per test/benchmark/stats.org); samtools version and flags not stated
hardware: Node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB memory at CRG per the sambamBench-nf README; CPU model not stated
why_faster: Parallelized BAM reading and writing (the README says that was the main advantage over samtools when Sambamba started in 2012); the README also says the D language suits HPC but gives no language-level mechanism.
stars_or_usage: 613 stars; over 250,000 Conda installs and over 1000 citations per README (January 2023)
tradeoffs: Implements an important subset of samtools functionality only (view, index, sort, markdup, depth, flagstat); GPL-2.0.
caveats: The README itself says samtools 1.4 (2017) reached parity and that Sambamba loses on sort; thread counts and samtools versions are not stated. The sambamBench-nf pipeline (guigolab) is public but its report page (guigolab.github.io and public-docs.crg.es) is blocked here and was not opened, so the per-operation table behind the README numbers is unverified. The Bioinformatics 2015 Sambamba paper was not reachable. Repo last commit is nearly two years old, so the numbers are not against current samtools releases.
found_via: WebSearch 'code.dlang.org D library benchmark faster than C++ ... samtools' led to the D ecosystem; opened the biod/sambamba README, test/benchmark/stats.org and guigolab/sambamBench-nf README

name: simd-adler32 (Rust) vs Wuffs adler32 (C)
baseline: Wuffs std/adler32 compiled to C with gcc (mingw64); not zlib, zlib-ng or libdeflate
workload: Adler-32 checksum of 10 KB and 100 KB random buffers, criterion benches in the repo plus 'wuffs bench -ccompilers=gcc -reps=1 -iterscale=300 std/adler32'.
claimed_speedup: README on Windows 10 with Intel i5-8300H: 10k buffer 43.805 GiB/s (212.61 ns) for simd-adler32 vs 2.63 GiB/s (3843 ns) for wuffs (16.7x, derived from page data); 100k buffer 33.320 GiB/s vs 2.6814 GiB/s (12.4x, derived from page data). Against the Rust crates in the same table: adler32 crate 1.9369 GiB/s (22.6x, derived from page data) and adler crate 530.43 MiB/s (about 85x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: rustc version and flags not stated; wuffs row built by the Wuffs bench tool with gcc under mingw64
hardware: Intel Core i5-8300H @ 2.30 GHz on Windows 10 Pro (a second table uses an i9-9880H MacBook Pro)
why_faster: Explicit SIMD (SSE, AVX, NEON, wasm) kernels selected at runtime.
tradeoffs: Runtime CPU dispatch; no_std; unsafe SIMD intrinsics inside.
caveats: Weak baseline: the wuffs row comes from a different harness (the Wuffs bench tool, marked with an asterisk in the README) on a 2018 laptop with gcc under mingw, and it is probably not the best C adler32 (zlib-ng, libdeflate and Chromium zlib have SIMD adler32 and were not tested). The cause of the 2.6 GiB/s Wuffs figure (scalar path versus SIMD path) is not stated. The macOS table lists only Rust crates.
found_via: crates.io API keyword listing 'simd accelerated' sorted by downloads; opened the README Performance section

name: simd-json (Rust port of simdjson) vs RapidJSON in serde-rs/json-benchmark
baseline: RapidJSON (C++), DOM parse in a nativejson-benchmark port run 256 times
workload: DOM parse and stringify of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json from nativejson-benchmark.
claimed_speedup: DOM parse MB/s, simd-json vs RapidJSON clang / gcc: twitter.json 810 vs 320 / 440 (2.5x and 1.8x, derived from page data); canada.json 380 vs 380 / 390 (parity); citm_catalog.json 720 vs 680 / 890 (1.06x faster than clang build, 0.8x of gcc build, derived). serde_json DOM parse is slower than RapidJSON on all three files (320 / 420 / 300 MB/s).
compiler_and_flags: Rust: rustc 1.59.0-nightly (2021-12-07), cargo run --release. C++: clang 11.0.0 and gcc 10.1.0, cpp/Makefile uses $(CXX) -std=c++1z -O3.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6600U @ 2.60 GHz (2015 laptop CPU); best of two runs on an idle machine
why_faster: Port of the simdjson SIMD parsing approach (crate README: 'Rust port of extremely fast simdjson JSON parser'); SIMD use is not matched, since the Rust crate relies on SIMD paths for a modern x86 CPU while the RapidJSON Makefile passes only -O3.
tradeoffs: Needs a modern x86 CPU with AVX2 or SSE4.2 (or NEON) for good results; the benchmark README says so; input buffers must be mutable and padded.
caveats: Numbers are from December 2021 (simd-json 0.4.11, old Rust and compilers) on a laptop CPU. RapidJSON is not the fastest C++ parser: C++ simdjson is faster than the Rust port (the README says the port tracks simdjson 0.2.x and aims for parity). Win is clear only on twitter.json; canada.json is parity and citm_catalog.json mixed. The benchmark repo's C++ Makefile passes only -std=c++1z -O3 (no -march flags) and RapidJSON SIMD defines were not checked. Evidence for an already catalogued project.
found_via: crates.io listing check of serde_json and simd-json; opened serde-rs/json-benchmark README and cpp/Makefile

name: Asdf (D, Mir) vs RapidJSON in kostya/benchmarks JSON
baseline: RapidJSON (C++); the number-accuracy-matched variant is 'RapidJSON Precise'
workload: kostya/benchmarks Json test: parse a large generated JSON file (/tmp/1.json) and compute a simple average over the coordinates.
claimed_speedup: Time in s (lower is better): D/ldc2 (Mir Asdf DOM) 0.133 vs C++/g++ RapidJSON 0.154 (1.16x) and C++/clang++ RapidJSON 0.194 (1.46x); vs the accuracy-matched RapidJSON Precise 0.212 (g++, 1.6x) and 0.262 (clang++, 2.0x) (ratios derived from page data). It is slower than simdjson On-Demand 0.060, simdjson DOM 0.103 to 0.107, DAW JSON Link 0.085 to 0.089 and gason 0.127 to 0.133.
compiler_and_flags: C++: g++ 16.1.0 and clang++ 22.1.8 (libc++) with -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto. D: ldc2 1.41.0, dub --build=release-nobounds with -mcpu=native -linkonce-templates -enable-cross-module-inlining, asdf ~>0.7.17 (json/test_mir_asdf.d and common/commands.mk opened).
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (kostya README Environment section), Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: D with the GC-free Mir containers; bounds checks are off in the benchmark build (release-nobounds); small ecosystem.
caveats: The Asdf test deserializes into a typed struct (deserialize!Avg) and the row is labelled DOM, while RapidJSON builds a full DOM, so the work may not be identical (the exact equivalence was not verified). The asdf README itself makes no speed comparison (it quotes 300+ MB/s read and write only). RapidJSON is not the fastest C++ option in the table (simdjson, DAW JSON Link and gason are faster). kostya notes that default (non-Precise) RapidJSON and non-Mir D parsers have number-parsing inaccuracies, which is why the Precise rows are the fair baseline. A neighbouring row, D/ldc2 (Mir Amazon's Ion DOM) from libmir/mir-ion, takes 0.220 s, about parity with g++ RapidJSON Precise 0.212. Evidence for an already catalogued project.
found_via: WebSearch 'code.dlang.org D library benchmark faster than C++' surfaced the D JSON benchmark threads; then the kostya/benchmarks README Json table, json/Makefile, json/test_mir_asdf.d and common/commands.mk

name: djvu-rs (Rust DjVu codec) vs DjVuLibre
baseline: DjVuLibre 3.5.29 (C++): ddjvu rendering and the c44 / cjb2 encoders
workload: Rendering DjVu pages (colour IW44 page at 150 dpi, bilevel JB2 page at 300 dpi, cold open plus decode plus render) and encoding (IW44 colour scan vs c44, lossless JB2 text page vs cjb2) on checked-in corpus files.
claimed_speedup: README Performance table (Apple M1 Max, same machine for both): render colorbook.djvu @150 dpi 4.46 ms vs 6.37 ms (1.4x); render cable_1973_100133.djvu @300 dpi 22.6 ms vs 36.8 ms (1.6x); cold open + decode + render colorbook.djvu 13.7 ms vs 41.6 ms (3.0x); IW44 colour encode vs c44 151 ms vs 474 ms (3.1x); lossless JB2 text page vs cjb2 7.0 ms vs 26.6 ms (3.8x). README headline: renders and encodes 1.4-3.8x faster than DjVuLibre.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.92.0 stable, release profile opt-level 3 with thin LTO (BENCHMARKS_RESULTS.md, opened); DjVuLibre build compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Apple M1 Max (10 cores), macOS 26.3.1, arm64
stars_or_usage: 11 stars; about 13k crates.io downloads of djvu-rs
tradeoffs: Clean-room MIT implementation written from the public DjVu v3 specification (no GPL code); encoder output is not always smaller than DjVuLibre (README: 1.025 to 1.040x c44 for IW44 and 0.952 to 1.011x cjb2); legacy BM44/PM44 pages are read-only.
caveats: First-party numbers on one Apple Silicon laptop; the baseline's compiler and flags are not stated. BENCHMARKS_RESULTS.md (encoder parity scorecard of 2026-07-13) contradicts the README claim of being faster on every encode case: goody two-shoes IW44 took 375.0 ms for djvu-rs vs 367.3 ms for c44, and in three rows djvu-rs output is much larger (cable JB2 4,720 B vs 2,248 B, Chinese cookbook 140 B vs 67 B, goody 440,864 B vs 327,798 B with PSNR 26.39 dB against 40.83 dB). The scorecard fastest rows (map atlas 29.6 ms vs 348.6 ms) differ from the README table rows, which are not in the scorecard. It appears the harness times the external c44 and cjb2 commands (process launch and file I/O included) against an in-process Rust encoder; this was not confirmed in the source. The benchmark dashboard on github.io is blocked here. The README table rows were not re-derived from the raw data. The full-workspace render numbers were rejected once as noisy and re-run, so the render rows come from targeted reruns.
found_via: crates.io API search q=djvu-rs (lead from the wave 14 notes on wasmlib claims); opened the README Performance table and BENCHMARKS_RESULTS.md via raw.githubusercontent.com
